newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish official says S&P upgrade unlikely for now.
newsitem.headline: Polish official says S&P upgrade unlikely for now.

text.p: Standard & Poor's decision to affirm Poland's credit ratings and revise its outlook to positive from stable means there is a chance of an upgrade in future, a Polish finance ministry official said on Tuesday.

"This means that we are perceived rather better than a year ago and we have a chance of an improvement of the rating in future," Wieslaw Szczuka, director of the ministry's foreign department, told Reuters. @

He declined to say when the ministry might expect such an upgrade but commented that Poland's current account deficit and the approach of parliamentary elections, expected in September, meant this was not a suitable moment for a change.
During the first quarter of 1997 Poland had a current account deficit of $1.5 billion against a $1.3 billion gap in all of 1996.

"There are two direct factors (preventing an upgrade). The first is a worsening of the external position of the balance of payments and the second is a degree of uncertainty, which...is always bound up with elections," Szczuka said.
But he added: "We are pleased with this modification and consider that every positive change is good, even if it takes place in small steps."

Standard & Poor's earlier announced in New York that it had affirmed Poland's BBB- long-term foreign currency rating and its A- long-term local currency rating, while revising the outlook to positive from stable on both.
It also affirmed the A-1 short-term local currency rating and assigned the A-3 short-term foreign currency rating.
The agency said factors behind its decision included prospects for inflation to sink to about 13-14 percent by end-1997 and possibly to single digits in 1998.

It praised recent progress on essential pension reforms and privatisation and said the ratio of net external debt of the general government to exports declined significantly last year and further reduction was expected this year.
Standard & Poor's noted progress in financial restructuring of state-owned commercial banks and a general strengthening of the financial system.

But factors holding Poland back included structural weakness in the politically sensitive agricultural sector, mining, and heavy industry, as well as an uncertain future pace of demonopolisation and privatization of large enterprises.
The agency pointed to the challenges of maintaining fiscal restraint while implementing expensive pension reform and said there was still a risk of delays in further reforms.
"A recent increase in current account deficit largely reflects capital imports accompanying ongoing restructuring and modernization of the economy," Standard & Poor's said.
It said financing the rising current account deficit should remain easily manageable without significantly eroding Poland's currency reserves, which have held stable over the last year.
